questions.stem: 10.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated until it decomposes completely: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Taking M(CaCO₃) = 100.1 g mol⁻¹, what mass of carbon dioxide is released?
questions.explanation: n(CaCO₃) = 10.0/100.1 = 0.0999 mol, which gives 0.0999 mol of CO₂, so m = 0.0999 × 44.0 = 4.40 g. 5.60 g is the mass of calcium oxide left behind; together the two products add to 10.0 g.

questions.stem: Iron(III) oxide is reduced in a blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Taking M(Fe₂O₃) = 159.6 g mol⁻¹, what mass of iron can be obtained from 16.0 g of Fe₂O₃?
questions.explanation: n(Fe₂O₃) = 16.0/159.6 = 0.100 mol, and each mole gives 2 mol of Fe, so m(Fe) = 0.200 × 55.8 = 11.2 g. Using a 1:1 ratio gives 5.59 g.

questions.stem: Excess silver nitrate is added to a 25.0 mL sample of sodium chloride solution, giving 0.717 g of dry silver chloride precipitate. Taking M(AgCl) = 143.4 g mol⁻¹, what was the concentration of the sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: n(AgCl) = 0.717/143.4 = 0.00500 mol, which equals n(NaCl) because Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl. c = 0.00500/0.0250 = 0.200 mol L⁻¹. 0.00500 mol L⁻¹ forgets to divide by the volume.

questions.stem: A 1.50 g sample of fertiliser containing ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄, is dissolved and treated with excess barium chloride. The dry barium sulfate precipitate weighs 2.33 g. Taking M(BaSO₄) = 233.4 and M((NH₄)₂SO₄) = 132.1 g mol⁻¹, what is the percentage of ammonium sulfate in the fertiliser?
questions.explanation: n(BaSO₄) = 2.33/233.4 = 0.00998 mol = n((NH₄)₂SO₄). Mass = 0.00998 × 132.1 = 1.32 g, so purity = 1.32/1.50 × 100 = 87.9%. 64.0% is the percentage of sulfate ions only, and 155% compares the precipitate mass directly with the sample mass.

questions.stem: 2.50 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄. Taking M(CuSO₄) = 159.6 g mol⁻¹, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Water lost = 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g = 0.0500 mol. n(CuSO₄) = 1.60/159.6 = 0.0100 mol. The ratio of water to CuSO₄ is 0.0500/0.0100 = 5, so the formula is CuSO₄·5H₂O.

questions.stem: Why is a hydrated salt heated repeatedly until its mass stops changing when finding its water of crystallisation?
options: To allow the salt to absorb moisture back from the air before weighing
To decompose the anhydrous salt into its separate elements
To make sure all of the water of crystallisation has been driven off
To make sure the salt has reacted completely with oxygen in the air
questions.explanation: If any water remains, the mass of water lost is underestimated and x comes out too small. Constant mass shows that no more water is being lost. The salt should not react with air or decompose; heating too strongly would cause errors.

questions.stem: In a gravimetric analysis, a student forgets to wash the precipitate with deionised water before drying and weighing it. How does this affect the calculated mass of the analyte?
options: It is too low, because some precipitate dissolves without washing
It is unaffected, because soluble salts evaporate when dried
It is too low, because the unwashed precipitate stays damp
It is too high, because soluble salts left on the precipitate add mass
questions.explanation: Washing removes dissolved spectator ions and excess reagent. Without it these dry onto the precipitate, so its mass, and the analyte mass calculated from it, is too high. Soluble salts do not evaporate, and leftover damp would raise the mass, not lower it.

questions.stem: 6.00 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.0 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess ethanol, producing 6.16 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.0 g mol⁻¹). What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: n(acid) = 6.00/60.0 = 0.100 mol, so the theoretical yield is 0.100 × 88.0 = 8.80 g of ester, and the percentage yield is 6.16/8.80 × 100 = 70.0%. 103% wrongly compares the product's mass with the reactant's mass.

questions.stem: A drug is made in two steps. The first step has a 80% yield and the second a 60% yield. What is the overall percentage yield?
questions.explanation: Only 80% of the starting material reaches the second step, and 60% of that becomes product: 0.80 × 0.60 = 0.48, or 48%. Averaging the two yields gives 70%, which overstates the outcome.

questions.stem: A student reports a 108% yield of aspirin from a synthesis. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The product had not been fully dried before it was weighed
Some of the product was lost on the filter paper
The reaction did not go all the way to completion
The reaction produced more mass than it used
questions.explanation: A yield above 100% means the weighed solid contains something besides pure product, most often water or solvent, or an impurity. Losses on filter paper and incomplete reaction both lower the yield, and mass is conserved in a reaction.

questions.stem: Why is the percentage yield of a synthesis usually below 100%, even when the procedure is followed correctly?
options: The product always absorbs water, which is removed before it is weighed
Side reactions occur, and some product is lost during separation and purification
Some mass is destroyed in every chemical reaction, as energy is released
The limiting reagent is always partly converted into the excess reagent
questions.explanation: Some reactant forms unwanted by-products, some reactions do not go to completion, and product is lost on glassware and during filtering or recrystallisation. Mass is conserved in chemical reactions.

questions.stem: When designing an esterification to maximise the yield of an expensive carboxylic acid's ester, which choice would help most?
options: Leaving out the concentrated sulfuric acid
Adding extra water to the reaction mixture
Using exactly equal amounts of each reactant
Using an excess of the cheaper alcohol
questions.explanation: Esterification is an equilibrium, so an excess of one reactant pushes it towards products and converts more of the expensive acid. Water is a product, so adding it lowers the yield, and the acid catalyst speeds the reaction to equilibrium.

questions.stem: Why is a solid product made in a synthesis often recrystallised before use?
options: To remove impurities and increase its purity
To increase the theoretical yield of the reaction
To convert the excess reagent into extra product
To make the product react faster when used
questions.explanation: Recrystallising dissolves the crude product in hot solvent and lets pure crystals form on cooling, while impurities stay in solution. It improves purity, though some product is always lost, so the actual yield falls slightly.

questions.stem: Which property must a substance have to be used as a primary standard?
options: It has a low molar mass so that small masses can be weighed
It is brightly coloured so that its end point is easy to see
It is very pure and does not absorb water or react with air
It is a strong acid or strong base that ionises completely
questions.explanation: A primary standard's mass must correspond exactly to a known number of moles, so it must be pure, stable and unaffected by moisture or carbon dioxide in the air. A high molar mass is preferred, because weighing errors are then a smaller fraction of the mass.

questions.stem: Why is solid sodium hydroxide not suitable as a primary standard?
options: It does not dissolve completely in water
It has too high a molar mass to weigh accurately
It absorbs water and reacts with carbon dioxide from the air
It is a weak base that only partly reacts with acids
questions.explanation: NaOH pellets take up water and react with CO₂, so a weighed mass contains an unknown amount of NaOH. Its solutions must instead be standardised by titration against a primary standard. NaOH is a strong, very soluble base.

questions.stem: 1.325 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate (M = 106.0 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved and made up to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. What is the concentration of the solution?
questions.explanation: n = 1.325/106.0 = 0.01250 mol, and c = 0.01250/0.2500 = 0.0500 mol L⁻¹. 0.0125 is the amount in moles, not the concentration, and 5.30 divides the mass rather than the moles by the volume.

questions.stem: Oxalic acid dihydrate, H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O (M = 126.0 g mol⁻¹), is a diprotic primary standard. What volume of 0.250 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide reacts exactly with 0.630 g of it?
questions.explanation: n(oxalic acid) = 0.630/126.0 = 0.00500 mol. It donates two protons, so n(NaOH) = 0.0100 mol and V = 0.0100/0.250 = 0.0400 L = 40.0 mL. Treating the acid as monoprotic gives 20.0 mL.

questions.stem: 20.0 mL of 0.500 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to 250.0 mL. What is the new concentration?
questions.explanation: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, so c₂ = 0.500 × 20.0/250.0 = 0.0400 mol L⁻¹. Diluting must lower the concentration, so 6.25 mol L⁻¹, from inverting the volumes, cannot be right. 0.0435 treats 250.0 mL as the volume of water added.

questions.stem: What volume of 2.00 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is needed to make 500.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution?
questions.explanation: V₁ = c₂V₂/c₁ = 0.100 × 500.0/2.00 = 25.0 mL of the stock solution, made up to 500.0 mL with water. 475 mL is the approximate volume of water added, not the volume of acid.

questions.stem: 2.43 g of magnesium is added to 50.0 mL of 2.00 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Which reactant is limiting, and how many moles of hydrogen form?
options: HCl is limiting; 0.0500 mol of H₂
Mg is limiting; 0.100 mol of H₂
HCl is limiting; 0.100 mol of H₂
Mg is limiting; 0.0500 mol of H₂
questions.explanation: n(Mg) = 2.43/24.3 = 0.100 mol and n(HCl) = 2.00 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol. Reacting all the Mg would need 0.200 mol of HCl, so HCl is limiting and gives 0.100/2 = 0.0500 mol of H₂. Comparing the mole amounts without the 1:2 ratio wrongly suggests a tie.

questions.stem: 50.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ barium chloride is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.300 mol L⁻¹ sodium sulfate. Taking M(BaSO₄) = 233.4 g mol⁻¹, what mass of barium sulfate precipitates?
questions.explanation: n(Ba²⁺) = 0.0100 mol and n(SO₄²⁻) = 0.0150 mol, reacting 1:1, so Ba²⁺ is limiting and 0.0100 mol of BaSO₄ forms: 0.0100 × 233.4 = 2.33 g. Using the sulfate amount gives 3.50 g, but there is not enough barium for that.

questions.stem: In a titration, what is the difference between the equivalence point and the end point?
options: Equivalence is when the indicator changes colour; the end point is when the burette is empty
Equivalence is when the pH reaches exactly 7; the end point is when all the acid has evaporated
Equivalence is reached at the start of a titration; the end point is reached at its finish
Equivalence is when reactants are in the exact mole ratio; the end point is the indicator's colour change
questions.explanation: The equivalence point is the theoretical point at which the reactants have been added in stoichiometric amounts. The end point is what is observed. A well-chosen indicator changes colour very close to the equivalence point. The pH at equivalence is 7 only for a strong acid with a strong base.

questions.stem: Why does an acid-base indicator change colour during a titration?
options: It is a weak acid whose acid and base forms have different colours
It reacts with the titrant to form a coloured precipitate
It is decomposed by excess acid into a coloured product
It is a strong acid that changes colour once it is neutralised
questions.explanation: An indicator HIn is a weak acid in equilibrium with its conjugate base In⁻, which has a different colour. As pH changes, the balance shifts from one form to the other, so the colour changes over a particular pH range.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide solution. Which indicator is most suitable?
questions.explanation: At equivalence the solution contains ethanoate ions, which are weakly basic, so the equivalence point is above pH 7. Phenolphthalein changes colour in this basic range; the other indicators would change colour well before equivalence.

questions.stem: Either methyl orange or phenolphthalein gives an accurate end point when hydrochloric acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide. Why?
options: Strong acids and bases need no indicator, so the choice makes no difference
The pH changes sharply over a wide range at equivalence, covering both indicators' ranges
Both indicators change colour at exactly pH 7 when used with strong acids
Hydrochloric acid reacts with each indicator to give the same coloured product
questions.explanation: For a strong acid with a strong base, one drop near equivalence moves the pH from about 3 to about 11, so any indicator changing colour in that range marks the end point within a drop. Neither indicator changes at pH 7 itself.

questions.stem: A 20.00 mL aliquot of sodium hydroxide solution is titrated with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid. The average titre is 18.40 mL. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.01840 = 0.00184 mol = n(NaOH), so c(NaOH) = 0.00184/0.02000 = 0.0920 mol L⁻¹. 0.109 comes from swapping the two volumes, and 0.00184 is the amount in moles.

questions.stem: A 25.00 mL aliquot of sulfuric acid is titrated with 0.150 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide, needing 22.60 mL: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid?
A 20.00 mL aliquot of 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ sodium carbonate is titrated with hydrochloric acid, needing 21.25 mL: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is the concentration of the acid?
questions.explanation: n(Na₂CO₃) = 0.0500 × 0.02000 = 0.00100 mol, so n(HCl) = 0.00200 mol and c = 0.00200/0.02125 = 0.0941 mol L⁻¹. Using a 1:1 ratio gives 0.0471 mol L⁻¹.

questions.stem: 10.00 mL of vinegar is diluted to 100.0 mL. A 20.00 mL aliquot of the diluted solution needs 16.80 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. What is the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.01680 = 0.00168 mol = n(CH₃COOH) in the aliquot, so the diluted solution is 0.00168/0.02000 = 0.0840 mol L⁻¹. The vinegar was diluted tenfold, so its concentration is 0.840 mol L⁻¹. Forgetting the dilution gives 0.0840.

questions.stem: Which piece of glassware is used to transfer an accurately known, fixed volume (an aliquot) of solution into a conical flask?
questions.explanation: A pipette delivers one fixed volume, such as 20.00 mL, very accurately. A burette delivers variable, measured volumes of the titrant, and measuring cylinders and beakers are far less accurate.

questions.stem: Before a titration, what should the conical flask be rinsed with?
options: The solution to be pipetted into it
questions.explanation: Water in the flask does not change the number of moles in the aliquot, so rinsing with deionised water is correct. Rinsing with either reacting solution would leave extra moles in the flask and make the titre wrong.

questions.stem: A student rinses the burette with deionised water but not with the hydrochloric acid it will hold, then titrates sodium hydroxide aliquots. How does this affect the calculated NaOH concentration?
options: It is too low, because the water reacts with the sodium hydroxide
It is too high, because the diluted acid gives larger titres
It is too low, because the diluted acid gives smaller titres
It is unaffected, because water does not take part in the reaction
questions.explanation: Water left in the burette dilutes the acid, so more of it is needed to neutralise each aliquot. The calculation assumes the original concentration, so it overestimates the moles of HCl and therefore the NaOH concentration.

questions.stem: Why are titrations repeated until three concordant titres are obtained?
options: To check the results are precise and reduce the effect of random errors
To remove any systematic error in the concentration of the titrant
To use up the standard solution so that none is wasted
To make the burette readings more accurate to the nearest 0.1 mL
questions.explanation: Concordant titres, typically within 0.10 mL of each other, show good precision, and averaging them reduces random error. Repeating cannot remove a systematic error such as a wrongly made standard, which affects every titre equally.

questions.stem: Why is no separate indicator needed when acidified potassium permanganate is used as the titrant?
options: Permanganate reacts with the analyte to form a white precipitate at the end point
Permanganate is a primary standard, so its end point is known in advance
The pH changes sharply at the end point, which a pH meter detects
Purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺, so the first excess drop turns the solution pink
questions.explanation: While the analyte remains, each drop of purple permanganate is decolourised as it is reduced to Mn²⁺. Once the analyte is used up, the next drop stays, giving a permanent pale pink end point. Permanganate is not a primary standard; it must be standardised.

questions.stem: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. A 20.00 mL aliquot of iron(II) solution needs 15.00 mL of 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ potassium permanganate. What is the concentration of Fe²⁺?

An iron tablet is dissolved in acid so that all its iron is present as Fe²⁺. The solution needs 18.00 mL of 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ KMnO₄ to reach the end point (MnO₄⁻ reacts with Fe²⁺ in a 1:5 ratio). What mass of iron did the tablet contain?
questions.explanation: n(MnO₄⁻) = 0.0200 × 0.01800 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol, so n(Fe) = 5 × 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.80 × 10⁻³ mol, and m = 1.80 × 10⁻³ × 55.8 = 0.100 g. Using a 1:1 ratio gives 0.0201 g, and 0.00180 is the amount of iron in moles.
